content.thinking:
I'm writing up the postmortem from the alert alone, since I can't read the metrics or know what users actually saw. The alert says the error rate went above threshold, so I'm leaning toward describing the symptom as io-shop requests failing with errors, while still weighing how much the alert really supports that.

I'm checking whether the causal chain goes further than the alert, and it doesn't: the only step is the error rate rising above threshold, backed by AL1. There's no change I can point to, and the flags only show absence of change, not a ruled-out cause, so I'll leave that list empty. I'm also starting on the contributing factors, where nobody being paged looks like a detection gap.

I'm listing the contributing factors now, and the first one is that nobody was paged, which looks like a detection gap. Argus also couldn't read io-shop's metrics or get any log lines for it, and the platform reported no pods, so the observability gap is what kept the cause from being found. There's a conflict to note too: the rollout shows three replicas, but the platform sees none, so pod placement isn't visible to Argus.

I'm now marking which contributing factors need an action item, and I'll propose one for each. The first is routing the io-shop error-rate alert to an on-call rotation so someone gets paged, and then I'll need a follow-up action for getting a person onto io-shop's current state with direct access to its metrics and logs.

I'm listing the remaining action items: a mitigation to have someone investigate io-shop's current state with direct access to its metrics and logs, then detection fixes so Argus can read io-shop's metrics, logs, and pod placement. I'm also noting a process item to record revision names in the deploy history.

I'm drafting the lessons section now, noting that Argus escalated instead of acting without evidence, and that the investigator widened the search for changes after finding none. I'm weighing whether anything went wrong there, and my conflicting pod and rollout readings are the one thing I'm still sorting out.

I'm weighing whether the Investigator's second log query (T16) was really a limit, since it re-read the 11:30 window already covered by T8 instead of reaching past the alert. That's a minor point about how the search was scoped, so I'm not sure it belongs under what went wrong.

I'm still on the causal chain: the step is that io-shop's callers saw requests fail, backed by the alert's error-rate reading, and I don't think the evidence goes any further than that. For the symptom I'm keeping it plain, io-shop requests failing with errors, and I'm noting that the alert's error rate is taken to reflect what users actually saw, since I couldn't read the metrics to confirm it. The dependencies in the service register went unchecked, so I'll leave them out, and I'm treating the alert time as the start of the incident.

action_items.item: Have a member of io-shop's owning team check io-shop's current error rate directly and find the cause of the failure, since the incident was escalated with no cause found.
Route the HighErrorRate alert for io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
Fix the metrics source so that Argus can read io-shop's per-minute metrics.
Fix log collection so that io-shop's log lines reach the store Argus queries.
Add an alert that fires when io-shop's metrics or log lines stop arriving.
Make io-shop's pod placement visible to Argus so that the platform's pod listing matches the replicas the rollout reports.
Record the revision name in io-shop's deployment history for every rollout.

causal_chain.step: io-shop requests failed: the HighErrorRate alert reported its error rate above threshold. No metrics, logs or change events that Argus read show why, so the evidence stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not routed to anyone on call. No on-call incident was linked, so nobody was paged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have started working on the failing service when the alert fired, instead of the incident ending in an escalation with nobody on it.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Argus could not read io-shop's per-minute metrics. The query came back with {T5.2} minutes (T5), so no onset, error rate or trend could be measured.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The onset and the size of the failure could have been measured and matched to a change or a dependency, and the cause found sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No io-shop log lines came back for the period before the alert. Both queries returned nothing (T9, T17).
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The errors themselves could have been read, which would have pointed to where the requests were failing.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: The platform reported no pods for io-shop (T7), but the rollout read shows {T13.2} replicas running (T13). Argus could not see where the replicas run.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Argus could have checked the failure against particular pods or nodes, which the Investigator said it needed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

contributing_factors.factor: The deployment history does not name the revision the io-shop replicas run (T13).
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The running revision could have been tied to a known change or ruled out.
contributing_factors.label: CF-5

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent widened its search for production changes after the first query found none.
Argus escalated the incident because the evidence was insufficient. It took no action on an unsupported cause.

input.still_at_risk: io-shop could keep failing requests with no person paged to see it.
